title: Modelling chocolate
subtitle: pliable chocolate paste for sculpting cake decorations
excerpt: Modelling chocolate is made by melting chocolate and stirring in glucose syrup until the mixture comes together into a pliable, clay-like paste. It sets firm at room temperature but softens from the warmth of your hands as you work with it, making it easy to roll, cut, and sculpt into flowers, ribbons, and figures for cake decoration.
sourceNotes: Modelling chocolate has been used by patissiers and cake decorators since at least the mid-20th century as an alternative to fondant and marzipan. It requires no drying time (unlike royal icing or gum paste) and has a better eating quality than fondant. The technique is standard in professional patisserie and has become popular in home baking through the 2000s and 2010s.

recipe.yieldDescription: enough to decorate one 20 cm cake
recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap tightly in cling film and freeze for up to 3 months. Defrost at room temperature and knead briefly to restore workability.
recipe.batchNotes: Scales directly by weight. Use 1 part chocolate to 1/3 part glucose syrup by weight as a reliable starting ratio.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 weeks ahead. Store wrapped in cling film at cool room temperature, not in the fridge.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thick, clear sugar syrup made from broken-down starch. In modelling chocolate it acts as a plasticiser, binding with the cocoa butter to create a pliable paste rather than a solid block.

content.text: Modelling chocolate is made by combining melted chocolate with
glucose syrup

. The syrup interferes with the cocoa butter crystallisation, producing a paste that stays soft enough to work with but holds its shape once released. It handles more like clay than fondant: you can pinch, roll, and sculpt it without the stickiness that makes fondant difficult.
Making the paste
Melt the chocolate

Chop 200 g of dark, milk, or white chocolate finely and melt over a bain-marie, stirring until smooth. Cool to 33°C for dark chocolate, 30°C for milk, 28°C for white. It should still be liquid but no longer feel hot on the back of your wrist. Overheated chocolate makes the paste grainy.
Add the glucose syrup

Warm 65 g of glucose syrup very briefly in a bowl set over hot water until it flows easily. Pour it all at once into the chocolate and stir with a spatula in short, deliberate strokes. The mixture will look broken and greasy at first. Keep working it: after about 30 seconds of stirring it will begin to come together into a smooth, glossy paste that pulls away from the sides of the bowl. Stop as soon as it coheres.
Rest before using

Scrape the paste onto a piece of cling film, press into a flat disc, wrap, and rest for at least 1 hour at room temperature. Fresh paste is too sticky to handle. The rest allows the glucose and cocoa butter to firm up to a workable consistency.
Working with modelling chocolate
Conditioning before sculpting

Break off a piece and knead it in your palms. Cold paste crumbles slightly at first; keep kneading and the warmth of your hands softens it quickly into a smooth, pliable ball. Work in portions: the rest of the paste should stay cool and firm while you work one section.
Rolling and cutting

Roll on a non-stick mat or smooth worktop. Modelling chocolate needs no icing sugar or cornflour to prevent sticking: the natural fat content of the cocoa butter prevents it from adhering. Roll to 2 to 3 mm thickness for petals and ribbons, 4 to 5 mm for ruffles. Cut with sharp cutters or a scalpel and lift with a palette knife.
Colouring

Use oil-based or powder food colouring. Water-based colouring causes the chocolate to seize. Start with a very small amount, knead to distribute, then assess. Colour darkens as it sets. For white modelling chocolate, any colour can be achieved; for dark chocolate, only deep tones are practical.
Troubleshooter

attrs.problem: Paste is greasy and separates when kneaded

content.text: The cocoa butter has separated. This usually means the chocolate was too warm when the glucose was added. Wrap the paste and refrigerate for 15 minutes to firm the fat, then knead again: it usually comes back together.

attrs.problem: Paste is stiff and crumbles even after warming

content.text: Too much glucose was used, or the paste is too cold. Microwave for 3 to 4 seconds at a time and knead immediately. Adding a small amount of extra glucose syrup (warmed) and kneading it in can also rescue very stiff paste.
